text:
In the late 1920s, London commuters navigating the Underground were handed geographically accurate maps that were, in practice, nearly useless. The lines wound and curved to reflect actual tunnel paths beneath the city. Stations in the dense centre were crushed together; outer stations sprawled wide. You could tell where things were, but not how to get there.
A young engineering draftsman in the Underground's Signals Office, working entirely on his own time and without commission, saw the problem clearly. Commuters did not need to know where stations sat in physical space — they only needed to know which direction to travel and where to change lines. Inspired by the electrical circuit diagrams he drew at work every day, he produced a redesign: lines only at horizontal, vertical, or 45-degree angles; the central area dramatically expanded for legibility; geographic fidelity abandoned entirely at the altar of clarity.
London Transport rejected his first submission in 1931 as "too revolutionary." A year later, they reconsidered. The 1933 print run was an instant public sensation. The same design principle was adopted by nearly every urban metro system on Earth. The draftsman spent much of the rest of his life attempting to recover proper authorship credit — London Transport had taken ownership of his idea for a modest one-time payment.
What was the name of this draftsman, and what principle of map design — deliberately sacrificing geographic accuracy for relational clarity — does his Underground map exemplify? Such maps are formally known as what?
The last name is also a name of a beer
